goal: Whoever builds or changes the product, a person or an AI, makes it give its users what they come for.

parts.what: The objectives, each with its key results, and a note that key results have no target values, because a measure made a target stops being a good measure (Goodhart's law), so they serve to judge how close the objective is.
Each objective, with an ID the rest of the document points to: one short sentence of what a user gets from the product, with the user as its subject.

Under each objective, two key results, each with an ID the rest of the document points to and the direction that is better: first how well the user gets what the objective says, then the lead time from when the user needs it, on their request or on an event, to having it. The first comes first: lead time is shortened only by changes that keep how well.
The participants, then one scenario for each objective.
Before the scenarios, in one place: each participant and whether it is a person, an AI or a script.

For one objective, named by its ID and a short name for how the user reaches it: the main path from when the user first needs it, on their request or on an event, to reaching it, laid out so the reader follows who does what, in order.

benefits.what: Reading an objective, does the developer know which user the product is for and what that user gets from it?
Weighing a piece of work, can the developer tell which one objective it brings closer?
After a change, can the developer tell from the key results whether users came closer to the objective?
Weighing a change that shortens the lead time, can the developer tell whether it keeps how well the user gets what the objective says?
For each objective, can the developer follow, step by step, how its user goes from when they first need it to having what the objective says?
Building a step of a scenario, can the developer tell whether it waits for a person, is taken by an AI, or runs as a script?
Can the developer change how the product works inside, while its users see the same, and leave the document as it is?

practices.thinking: An objective is the progress one user is trying to make, said from where they stand, not what the product does.
steps: List each one who comes to the product with a goal of their own, a person or an AI, by the role they play.
Write each one's objective as one sentence that fits on one line: that user as its subject, then a verb, its object and the context it is done in, with no feature or mechanism of the product.
Ask whether the product could do all the sentence says while that user is no better off; if so, rewrite the sentence around what the user gains.

practices.thinking: Objectives are cut so that each piece of work brings one of them closer, no gain is written twice, and none is left out.
steps: List each user and what each gets from the product, and give each pair one objective; merge objectives that one piece of work would bring closer together, and split an objective that holds gains a piece of work could bring closer apart, until each piece of work brings exactly one closer.
Take each change planned or recently made that alters what a user gets, and name the one objective it brings closer.

practices.thinking: A key result counts what users do or feel as they come closer to the objective, so it cannot get better while they get nothing more.
steps: For the objective, list how success or failure would show in what the user does or feels, such as giving up, undoing a result or working around the product.

Turn the signs kept into two measures, each a share, an average per user, a count or a time, and name what it is counted out of: one of how well the user gets what the objective says, and the lead time from when the user needs it, on their request or on an event, to having it.
Ask whether all the objective's key results could get better while the user still does not get what the objective says; if so, add or rework key results until they could not.

practices.thinking: A scenario is one run of the main path to the objective, the one most users take, from the request that starts it to the gain that ends it.
steps: Name each scenario by its objective's ID and a short active verb phrase, the user its subject, saying how they reach it.
Write each step as one message, from the one who takes it to the one it acts on, saying what it passes, checks or changes, such as an arrow in a Mermaid sequence diagram.
Mark a part that repeats as a loop with its condition, holding each step that repeats.
Read the scenario from start to end: the first message is the user's request, the last gives the user the end, and each step moves toward it.
